briefs.bodyText:
Core sector grew 7.9% in Sept, compared with 3.1% a year ago, driven by strong performance in electricity, cement and refinery products and aided by a favourable base as well, official data released Tuesday showed. Sequentially, the growth marked acceleration from an upwardly revised figure of 5.9% in Aug. This is the strongest performance of the core sector in the new series with the revised base year.
Output in the energy-dominant industries like natural gas (-4.6%), crude oil (-1.4%) and fertilisers (-11.7%) saw continued sequential contraction, reflecting the impact of the prolonged conflict in West Asia. Output in the refinery products (10.3%) and coal (10.7%), however, saw acceleration during the month.
Output in the infrastructure-dominant industries such as electricity (11.4%) and steel (4.9%) showed positive growth in Sept. In the newly added iron ore industry, output further accelerated (18.4%) during the month.
Bank of Baroda chief economist Madan Sabnavis said Sept figures highlight buoyancy in infrastructure where govt has been spending.

briefs.headline: SpaceX, Tesla boards weigh $3.5 trillion merger; Elon Musk endorses idea
briefs.deck: SpaceX is valued at more than $2 trillion, while Tesla has a market value of about $1.5 trillion. When asked on the call about the prospects of merging the two companies, Musk initially said he was “tap dancing through a minefield” before going into more detail. He cautioned that getting enough support from Tesla shareholders may be tricky and that neither committee has settled on terms.
briefs.bodyText:
Elon Musk
 openly endorsed the prospect of combining SpaceX with Tesla Inc in what would be the biggest-ever corporate merger, uniting assets from electric cars to AI data centres to rocket and satellite capabilities. The world’s richest man said Tuesday the boards of both companies had formed special committees of independent directors to consider the idea.
“There’s a lot of merit to combining the companies,” Musk said on a conference call after SpaceX announced earnings that beat estimates.
SpaceX is valued at more than $2 trillion, while Tesla has a market value of about $1.5 trillion. When asked on the call about the prospects of merging the two companies, Musk initially said he was “tap dancing through a minefield” before going into more detail. He cautioned that getting enough support from Tesla shareholders may be tricky and that neither committee has settled on terms.
Musk Endorses Idea Which Would Result InThe World’s Biggest-Ever Corporate Union
“I think it would be a good idea, but it’s really up to the special committees of both companies,” Musk said, adding he can’t be part of the discussions because he’s a conflicted party.
SpaceX and Tesla shares both extended gains in late trading after Musk’s comments. SpaceX stock jumped 10% shortly after the open Wednesday, while Tesla rose as much as 3.5%.
A merger of SpaceX and Tesla would be a blockbuster, creating a conglomerate spanning electric vehicles, energy storage batteries, rockets and satellites. The stated rationale for bringing those disparate interests together lies in their shared ambitions to leverage artificial intelligence for data centres in space, driverless cars and humanoid robots.
“There’s no question that Musk wants the merger, and he wants to get it done sooner rather than later,” said Gene Munster, founder of Deepwater Asset Management, which has invested in both companies. “It was a key question on the call, and Elon said it was a good idea about three times. He’s getting people excited about it, and he wants to bump up the enthusiasm.”
Musk made the comments after SpaceX posted $4.4 billion in net income for the quarter ended in September, far better than analysts’ average projection of $1.88 billion. Revenue increased 161% from a year ago and also beat expectations.
Revenue from SpaceX’s AI business soared to $7.56 billion in the quarter, more than nine times what the company generated a year ago.

briefs.headline: Surge in gold loans partly reflects stress, say lenders
briefs.deck: During the company’s Q2FY27 earnings, Piramal Finance MD & CEO Jairam Sridharan said 15% to 23% of gross gold loan disbursements across the industry over the past year went to customers already more than 90 days overdue. Piramal’s policy bars lending to such borrowers. According to RBI data, gold loans accounted for a third of incremental retail lending in Q1FY27.
briefs.bodyText:
MUMBAI: A surge in gold loans may partly reflect borrower stress, with lenders allowing customers already in deep delinquency to borrow against gold and repay overdue loans, Macquarie said in a report. The trend raises questions about whether gold-backed lending is driven by consumption or income-generating needs or is merely helping borrowers manage debt by shifting loans.
During the company’s Q2FY27 earnings, Piramal Finance MD & CEO Jairam Sridharan said 15% to 23% of gross gold loan disbursements across the industry over the past year went to customers already more than 90 days overdue. Piramal’s policy bars lending to such borrowers.
The trend raises questions about whether gold-backed lending is driven by consumption or income-generating needs or is merely helping borrowers manage debt by shifting loans.
In its earnings call last week, Bajaj Finance said it was moving away from short-tenor gold loans, which can trigger accidental delinquencies when customers fail to repay the full principal and interest on time. The company prefers longer tenors that offer borrowers greater flexibility.
“Auction is not liked by any constituent... so it’s better to manage it through risk rather than manage it through auction is how we have taken a position to be,” a company official said.
According to RBI data, gold loans accounted for a third of incremental retail lending in Q1FY27. Suresh Ganapathy, an analyst at Macquarie, said gold had become the second-largest retail loan book after mortgages, accounting for 28% of non-housing retail loans.
Citing Piramal’s comments on borrower stress, he said collections teams at other banks and NBFCs could be directing overdue borrowers to pledge gold and borrow from another lender to clear existing NPAs.
He also cautioned that many lenders were rushing into the business without fully recognising the accompanying risks.

briefs.headline: Jio IPO subscribed within 100 mins; subscribed over 3x on Day 1
briefs.deck: The institutional (QIB) part of the IPO, in which a little over 4.9 crore shares were offered, was subscribed nearly 9.5 times while the high-net-worth investors’ portion, in which about 3.6 crore shares were reserved, was subscribed 1.7 times. Usually, in most initial offerings, institutional players apply on the last day of the offer.
briefs.bodyText:
MUMBAI: The maiden public offering for Jio Platforms was subscribed within 100 minutes of opening as institutional buyers led the charge. At close of the session on Day 1, the Rs 30,213-crore IPO, the biggest in India’s capital market history, was subscribed over three times, data from bourses showed.
The institutional (QIB) part of the IPO, in which a little over 4.9 crore shares were offered, was subscribed nearly 9.5 times while the high-net-worth investors’ portion, in which about 3.6 crore shares were reserved, was subscribed 1.7 times. Usually, in most initial offerings, institutional players apply on the last day of the offer.
Institutional buyers lead with 9.5X bidding
Exchange data also showed that the portion reserved for employees was subscribed 1.4 times while the part reserved for 
Reliance Industries
 shareholders was subscribed 1.5 times. Only the retail part, in which about 8.5 crore shares are being offered, was not fully subscribed on Day 1. This portion closed the opening day at a 70% subscription level.
At the close of Day 1, the total demand for Jio shares was worth about Rs 3.2 lakh crore, including the anchor portion.
The strong response to the offering comes largely on the back of a Rs 2.5 lakh crore subscription to the anchor book, 30 times the book’s size of Rs 8,110 crore, disclosures by merchant bankers to the issue showed.
In the IPO, Jio Platforms is offering 27 crore shares at a per-share price band of Rs 1,065 to Rs 1,119. 
Of the total number of shares on offer, a little over 7.2 crore shares were offered to institutional buyers through the anchor book while a little over 19.7 crore shares are on offer through the bidding process. The bidding will close on Friday, Oct 23, and shares are expected to be listed on Oct 28.
Marquee global and domestic investors, aggregating 212, participated in the anchor part. The anchor book was led by a Rs 500-crore bid by domestic life insurance major Life Insurance Corporation. Among the top global investors were BNP Paribas, which put in funds worth Rs 303 crore, and BlackRock, which, through six of its funds, put in Rs 128 crore.

briefs.headline: The broken promise of the right to work
briefs.deck: The replacement of MGNREGA with the VB-GRAM G Act has weakened the rural right-to-work framework; restoring a meaningful right to work through adequate funding, living wages and stronger local institutions would advance constitutional aims while also supporting rural demand and economic growth
briefs.bodyText:
On August 21, a three-judge Supreme Court Bench led by the Chief Justice of India dismissed a petition and sought a fresh one in a case on minimum wages in rural employment guarantee programmes. The Bench lauded MGNREGA’s role in rural development. It probed whether the ‘Right to Work’ should be treated on par with Article 21, the fundamental right to life, sparking an important discussion on the constitutional foundations of this right.
A guarantee under strain
Despite its limited scope of only 100 days of work per rural household and chronic underfunding, the Mahatma Gandhi National Rural Employment Guarantee Act (MGNREGA) was the only law anchored in the core principle of the right to work. In December 2025, the Union government replaced MGNREGA with the Viksit Bharat — Guarantee for Rozgar & Ajeevika Mission (Gramin) (VB-GRAM G) Act, and its implementation began on July 1. About 3.44 crore households worked for about 44 crore person-days under MGNREGA in July and August, on average, over the previous five years (Table 1). There has been a 68% decrease in employment in July and August this year compared with the average of the preceding five years. Notwithstanding the proverbial ‘teething issues’, the dismantling of MGNREGA’s demand-driven right-to-work framework and the disproportionate fiscal burden that the new law places on States are likely to be major factors behind the dramatic fall in employment under the VB-GRAM G Act.
The impact of taking away even this limited right to work is therefore palpable. Discussions around the recent Supreme Court observations on the right to work can be traced back to the Constituent Assembly debates.
While most members agreed that a right to work was vital, the debate rested on whether it should be a fundamental right or be part of the Directive Principles of State Policy (DPSP). The DPSPs do not automatically constitute rights but are meant to serve as precepts for governments to formulate laws and policies. This became the basis of the differences in perspective.
Professor K.T. Shah had strongly advocated recognising the right to work as a fundamental right, arguing that the State needed a constitutional and positive legal mandate to guarantee socio-economic security to its citizens. Dr. B.R. Ambedkar, among others, held that while the right to work was an essential goal, its immediate universal enforcement was not fiscally and institutionally viable in a newly independent India that had been hollowed out of its resources. The placement of the right within the Directive Principles, rather than among the fundamental rights, thus reflected a deliberate constitutionalism of aspiration, rather than an abandonment of the welfare ideal. As scholars Anjani Kapoor and Manu Bhagwan have written in their essay ‘Ambedkar and the anti-isolation of Fellowship’, “The constitution does not establish the nation, but rather provides the tools to help achieve it.”
Therefore, Article 41 of the DPSP states: ‘The State shall, within the limits of its economic capacity and development, make effective provision for securing the right to work…” Embodying stronger progressive consecrations, Articles 39, 42 and 43 call for the “right to an adequate means of livelihood, equal pay for equal work for both men and women, just and humane conditions of work” and to “secure to all workers a living wage and decent standard of life.”
From aspiration to a statutory right
The Supreme Court, in Olga Tellis vs Bombay Municipal Corporation (1985), ruled that the right to livelihood was a necessary condition for the fundamental right to life, giving a judicial fillip to the right to work. Spurred by the collective efforts of activists and rural workers, the National Rural Employment Guarantee Act was passed in 2005. Although limited in scope, it made a pan-India right-to-work law a reality for the first time. The State had to ensure its statutory obligation to provide employment at minimum wages.
In 2009, MGNREGA wages were delinked from the Minimum Wages Act, 1948. Over time, MGNREGA wages barely kept pace with inflation and continued to remain lower than the minimum agricultural wages in most States. Low wages and an inadequate budget for generating employment have resulted in a steep decline in household earnings, with estimated total household earnings halving in July and August this year compared with the same months last year (Figure 1).
During the recent hearing, the Supreme Court Bench remarked that if financial resources remained the same, having a minimum wage threshold could reduce the number of workers who could be provided employment. This remark, which appears to align with the Union government’s approach to employment guarantee, merits scrutiny on at least two counts.
First, it vitiates the judgment in Sanjit Roy vs State of Rajasthan (1983) where the Supreme Court observed that payment of wages below minimum wages violates Article 23 of the Constitution and is akin to ‘forced labour.’ Second, it rests on a misleading economic logic that financial resources to implement a welfare programme must remain unchanged and constrained.
In reality, higher wages for rural workers increase their purchasing power, enhance their freedoms, and improve human development outcomes. These, in turn, increase effective demand for goods and services, creating a positive multiplier effect, resulting in higher economic productivity. Therefore, higher government spending on an employment guarantee programme at increased wages can yield a mutually reinforcing cycle between development and growth.
A retreat from the right to work
By putting an arbitrary cap on funds for the VB-GRAM G Act and not linking it with minimum wages, the very notion of employment guarantee stands delegitimised. States are already grappling with fiscal constraints and curtailed borrowing limits under the Fiscal Responsibility and Budget Management (FRBM) framework. The increased burden of funding the VB-GRAM G Act will prevent States from generating employment. The sharp drop in employment and earnings is a reflection of this change.
The VB-GRAM G Act also contains provisions to denotify certain areas and exclude them from the scheme, thereby limiting the universality of MGNREGA’s right to work.
Lawyer Purbayan Chakraborty highlights how the Supreme Court has affirmed the doctrine of non-retrogression in Navtej Singh Johar vs Union of India. The doctrine implies that once the State has achieved a certain level of progressive legislation and enforceability of a right, it cannot implement measures that deliberately undo it. Non-retrogression operates as a check on State power, ensuring that rights, once realised, are not diluted later. The replacement of MGNREGA with the VB-GRAM G Act appears to be in violation of this doctrine.
Rural wages have been stagnant for a decade, while women are increasingly employed as ‘unpaid family workers’. In such light, the minimal requirements for affirming the commitment to the right to work are: linking MGNREGA wages to living wages, timely payment of wages, a focus on social audits by empowering local institutions to be partners in mitigating corruption, and giving more powers to Panchayati Raj institutions.
All these measures could be implemented within a legal framework of the right to work. The VB-GRAMG Act, unfortunately, is silent on most of them. Reinstating the right to work would therefore not only be a legal course correction advancing constitutional aims, but would also be sound economics.
(The authors are affiliated with the Centre for the Study of the Indian Economy, Azim Premji University. The views expressed are personal)

stories.headline: Rabada scripts history, reaches rare Test milestone in fewer balls than Steyn
stories.deck: In 38 home Tests, Rabada has taken 200 wickets at an average of 20.06. He joins Dale Steyn (261 wickets), Makhaya Ntini (249) and Shaun Pollock (235) on the list.
stories.bodyText:
Kagiso Rabada
 became only the fourth South African bowler to take 200 Test wickets on home soil, joining some of the country's biggest names in the record books.
Rabada, who returned to competitive cricket for the first time since the Indian Premier League (IPL) final, dismissed Nic Maddinson and Mitchell Starc in the first innings to finish with figures of 2/33 in 12 overs.
In 38 home Tests, Rabada has taken 200 wickets at an average of 20.06. His record includes 10 five-wicket hauls and four ten-wicket hauls, with best bowling figures of 7/112. He joins 
Dale Steyn
 (261 wickets), 
Makhaya Ntini
 (249) and Shaun Pollock (235) on the list.
Only Steyn reached 200 home Test wickets in fewer matches, taking 37 Tests compared to Rabada's 38. However, Rabada reached the milestone in just 7,017 balls, the fewest by any bowler, surpassing Steyn's 7,751.
Overall, Rabada has taken 342 wickets in 74 Tests at an average of 22.01. He has 17 five-wicket hauls and four ten-wicket hauls, with best figures of 7/112. He is South Africa's fourth-highest wicket-taker in Test cricket.
Meanwhile, South Africa fought back in the ongoing Test by bowling Australia out for just 99 in their first innings and enforcing the follow-on. Steven Smith was the only Australian batter to score 20 or more, making 28 off 88 balls with two fours. 
Marco Jansen led the attack with 5/33, while Rabada took 2/33 and Wiaan Mulder returned figures of 2/13.
South Africa had also faced difficulties with the bat earlier in the match, slipping to 110/6 on the third day after rain had allowed little play over the first two days. Captain Temba Bavuma then led the recovery with 179 off 334 balls, including 18 fours and a six.
Bavuma first added 132 runs with Jansen, who scored 85 off 100 balls with nine fours and three sixes. He then put on another 183 runs with Simon Harmer, who made 82 off 157 balls, hitting 10 fours and a six. Their efforts took South Africa to 425/9 declared, a turnaround after Scott Boland's 5/81 had put the hosts under pressure.
Australia currently lead the three-match series 1-0. With one day remaining in the Test, South Africa have a chance to level the series at 1-1.

stories.headline: Arshdeep set to become first Indian to achieve this feat
stories.deck: Arshdeep Singh is just five wickets away from becoming the first Indian bowler to claim 150 wickets in T20 internationals ahead of the five-match series against New Zealand. The left-arm pacer has taken 145 wickets in 99 T20Is and is also closing in on 300 wickets in T20 cricket overall.
stories.bodyText:
Arshdeep Singh
 is on the verge of creating history as India prepare for their five-match T20I series against New Zealand, with the left-arm pacer needing just five more wickets to become the first Indian bowler to reach 150 wickets in the format.
The series begins on Thursday, with the opening T20I scheduled to be played in Christchurch. Arshdeep is expected to be an important part of India's plans across the five matches after recovering from a shoulder blow sustained during the fourth T20I against the West Indies. He was included in the playing XI for the fifth T20I in Bengaluru, although that match was washed out by rain.
Since making his T20I debut in 2022, Arshdeep has established himself as one of India's leading bowlers in the shortest format. He became the country's highest T20I wicket-taker at the start of 2025 and has continued to add to his tally.
In 99 T20Is, the Punjab Kings pacer has claimed 145 wickets at an average of 20.30. His record includes two four-wicket hauls and a five-wicket haul, with best figures of 5/51.
Five more wickets would make Arshdeep the ninth bowler overall to reach 150 T20I wickets and the first Indian to achieve the feat. Afghanistan's Rashid Khan currently leads the all-time list with 197 wickets in 118 matches.
Arshdeep has already enjoyed success against New Zealand, taking 17 wickets in 10 T20Is at an average of 20.00. His tally against the Black Caps includes a four-wicket haul and a five-wicket haul, with his best figures of 5/51.
In New Zealand, he has picked up four wickets in two T20Is. His best performance on Kiwi soil came in Napier in 2022, where he returned figures of 4/37.
Arshdeep is also approaching a significant milestone in T20 cricket across all levels. Having taken 288 wickets in 223 T20 matches, he needs 12 more to reach 300 wickets in the format.
His performances in T20Is this year have further underlined his importance to the Indian attack. He has collected 35 wickets in 27 matches at an average of 24.68 and an economy rate of 9.20, including a five-wicket haul and best figures of 5/51.
With two milestones within reach, Arshdeep will be looking to make his mark against New Zealand and become the first Indian to enter the 150-wicket club in men's T20 internationals.

stories.headline: Suma Shirur unveils Axis Bank Lakshya Shooting Club HPC
stories.bodyText:
The red state transport bus that once took Suma Shirur from Panvel to Dadar and beyond for practice has come to symbolise how far the Olympian has travelled in her pursuit of creating a better ecosystem for Indian shooters.
Twenty years after starting the Lakshya Shooting Club, Shirur on Wednesday unveiled the Axis Bank Lakshya Shooting Club High Performance Centre in Belapur. Olympic medallist Gagan Narang inaugurated the seven-storied facility in the presence of six other Olympians and several shooting stalwarts.
Equipped with two modern shooting ranges, a sports science laboratory, a gym, a mind gym, a Pilates studio, residential accommodation and a lounge, the centre is designed as a one-stop destination for aspiring shooters.
Supported by Axis Bank and the Government of Maharashtra, it aims to provide athletes with the infrastructure and expertise needed to compete at the highest level.
“Like all the Olympians from my generation will agree, we never had access to anything. We only saw others using it and wished we had the same,” Shirur said. “I would like to create things that I never got.”
The former India coach said her ambition extended beyond building a facility for Lakshya’s own athletes.
“I don’t want them to run around the world. I want them to come here and be a part of Lakshya Shooting Club,” she said, emphasising that the centre would welcome shooters aspiring to represent India.
She intends to begin with a small cohort of six to eight residential athletes, alongside a high-performance programme for those on the brink of international competition and a development squad for talented shooters aged 13 to 19.
Years of hard work
Narang, who cut the ribbon, said the facility was the product of years of hard work, sacrifice and belief. He also highlighted the role played by Shirur’s husband, Siddharth, an architect who helped translate her vision into a physical space.
“Your circumstances may limit your resources. But they should never limit your dreams,” Narang told the young athletes.
For Shirur, the next challenge is to make the centre sustainable and ensure that financial constraints do not prevent talented shooters from accessing it. She also hopes to integrate technology more deeply into training, helping coaches analyse performance and accelerate athletes’ development.
“This is just the beginning,” she said, looking towards a future in which the centre helps Indian shooting become a global powerhouse.
“I would like to create things that I never got”

briefs.headline: On-song India look to beat travel fatigue in T20 series-opener against New Zealand
briefs.deck: Most recent T20 clash on New Zealand soil was in 2022 in Napier, where the rain-interrupted match ended in a tie via the Duckworth-Lewis method
briefs.bodyText:
Unbeaten in their last two T20 series, the Shreyas Iyer-led India would rely heavily on their batting firepower to outwit New Zealand even though the relatively inexperienced tourists have got barely two days to rest, acclimatise and train for the five-match rubber beginning here on Thursday (October 22, 2026).
Their most recent T20 clash on New Zealand soil was in 2022 in Napier, where the rain-interrupted match ended in a tie via the Duckworth-Lewis method. The series, however, was claimed by India, who managed to win the only game that was not wrecked by inclement weather.
In the line-up of batters chosen for the upcoming assignment, only four have previously played T20Is in New Zealand. That includes skipper Iyer, Ishan Kishan, Sanju Samson, and Shivam Dube.
Therefore, even though the likes of Abhishek Sharma, Tilak Varma and 15-year-old sensation Vaibhav Sooryavanshi are known marauders, the nippy and seaming conditions in this part of the world would need some adjustment.
For Iyer, the challenge would be to prove himself in a challenging away assignment after his tenure began with back-to-back losses in Ireland and England.
Mitchell Santner's New Zealand would be eager to make it as difficult as possible for Iyer, who is coming here after India's second successive gold-winning run at the Asian Games and a drawn hard-fought home series against the West Indies.
However, if the New Zealand series follows the script that unfolded in the U.K. earlier this year, pressure will only mount on Iyer, who is expected to lead India in the T20 World Cup to be held in Australia and New Zealand in two years' time.
A confident Iyer said his team is used to playing in different conditions, having taken a long flight from India hours after sharing the home series against the West Indies.
India are also without two proven match-winners in injured all-rounder Hardik Pandya, who led the team when they toured in 2022, and pace spearhead Jasprit Bumrah, who will only play ODIs and Tests in this tour.
However, even though Sooryavanshi is likely to warm the bench, the batting is oozing with firepower as demonstrated by Abhishek and Samson in the home assignment against the west Indies. By Iyer's own admission, it is the bowling that needs fixing.
The return of veteran pacer Bhuvneshwar Kumar after nearly four years and fit-again mystery spinner Varun Chakravarthy should solve part of the problem but questions remain over the abilities of all-rounders Nitish Kumar Reddy and Shivam Dube.
India like to bat till number eight and they are unlikely to shed that mindset to strengthen their bowling.
New Zealand captain Santner expects the conditions to vary over the course of the series but said offering flat tracks to a power-packed India may not be the best strategy. He would hope that his own big-hitters like Glenn Phillips and Finn Allen outperform the Indian stars.
The injury-forced absence of Rachin Ravindra opens up an opportunity for veteran Devon Conway to move up the order.
"If there is something in the pitch for the seamers to start, it's obviously nice, but throughout the series we're going around the country, they're not all going to be green seamers and flying around. So both teams are going to have to adapt quickly to the conditions and then play accordingly," Santner said.
Given the expectedly pace-friendly conditions, New Zealand has variety with strong options in Jacob Duffy, Matt Henry, Adam Milne, Lockie Ferguson, Kyle Jamieson and Blair Tickner.
But despite the jet lag, India would be overwhelming favourites to come good. The two countries are celebrating 100 years of sporting ties this year and the T20Is would be followed by a five-match ODI series and two Tests.

India: Shreyas Iyer (c), Abhishek Sharma, Sanju Samson, Vaibhav Sooryavanshi, Ishan Kishan, Tilak Varma, Axar Patel, Shivam Dube, Nitish Kumar Reddy, Naman Dhir, Prince Yadav, Mayank Yadav, Arshdeep Singh, Bhuvneshwar Kumar, Varun Chakaravarthy, Kuldeep Yadav.

briefs.headline: Sindhu survives scare to advance at French Open
briefs.deck: Sindhu started strongly, taking the opening game 21-14, but Katethong fought back in the second, dominating the rallies to level the match with a commanding 21-8 win
briefs.bodyText:
India's double Olympic medallist P.V. Sindhu survived a scare from Thailand's world No. 26 Supanida Katethong to advance in the French Open Super 750 badminton tournament here on Wednesday (October 21 2026).
The former world champion and world No. 1 battled for an hour and four minutes before prevailing 21-14, 8-21, 23-21 in a gruelling encounter.
Sindhu started strongly, taking the opening game 21-14, but Katethong fought back in the second, dominating the rallies to level the match with a commanding 21-8 win.
The decider proved to be a tense affair, with both players fighting for every point. Sindhu eventually held her nerve in the closing stages to edge past the Thai shuttler 23-21 and seal her place in the next round.
Reflecting on the hard-fought win, Sindhu admitted it was far from her best performance but was relieved to get through.
"Some matches you just have to find a way to win. Today was one of those," she said.
"Credit to Supanida, she made me fight for every point. I felt like I was trying to impose my game throughout, but somehow things kept slipping away. Will go through the footage and see what needs to change," she added.
Sindhu also recalled a crucial challenge late in the decider, when a close line call went against her.
"Even that challenge at 21-20, the shuttle clipping the line by a hair's breadth! Some days God really makes you fight for it," she said.
"I needed this win. End of story. Not the prettiest, plenty to reflect on, but happy to be through. Recovery underway, another battle tomorrow. One match at a time," Sindhu added.
In another women's singles match, Unnati Hooda bowed out after losing 18-21, 21-12, 17-21 to Japan's Riko Gunji.
Ayush Shetty rallies to beat Srikanth
Ayush Shetty fought back from a game down to beat Kidambi Srikanth 19-21, 21-16, 21-12 in under an hour to advance to the next round in the men's singles.
Meanwhile, India's top-ranked men's singles player and former world championships bronze medallist Lakshya Sen gave a walkover to world No. 9 Kodai Naraoka of Japan in the opening round.
Lakshya has suffered early exits at the World Championships, the Asian Games and the recently-concluded Denmark Open.

briefs.headline: India to open U19 Women's T20 World Cup campaign against West Indies
briefs.deck: The third edition of the tournament will feature four groups of four teams each, with matches scheduled across venues in Chattogram, Sylhet and Kathmandu
briefs.bodyText:
India will begin their ICC U19 Women's T20 World Cup title defence against the West Indies in Kathmandu on January 22.
The International Cricket Council (ICC) on Wednesday (October 21, 2026) announced the schedule for the U19 Women's T20 World Cup, which will be played in Bangladesh and Nepal from January 21 to February 6.
The third edition of the tournament will feature four groups of four teams each, with matches scheduled across venues in Chattogram, Sylhet and Kathmandu.
Two-time champions India have been clubbed alongside co-hosts Nepal, West Indies and Ireland in Group A.
Co-hosts Bangladesh and UAE will play the tournament opener on January 21 while Australia, the runners-up at the previous edition, take on Nigeria in Sylhet on the same day.
In Kathmandu, Sri Lanka will play Scotland at Upper Mulpani International Cricket Ground, followed by England against the USA.
Nepal will open their campaign against Ireland on January 22. New Zealand will face Samoa and South Africa will take on Pakistan in Chattogram on the same day.
ICC CEO, Sanjog Gupta, said: "The ICC U19 World Cup is the stage that showcases the future of our sport and serves as the ultimate platform for young players to make the leap towards elite careers representing their countries.
"The choice of our hosts — Bangladesh and Nepal — is also reflective of the ICC's belief and investment in the future of the cricket ecosystem.
"With deep passion for cricket and nearly 40% of the two countries' populations below the age of 20, they serve as the ideal hosts for one of the world's biggest youth sporting events," he added.
The group stage will run through January 26 after which the qualifying teams will advance to the Super Six stage.
The teams will then be divided into two groups, with the top two sides progressing to the semi-finals, scheduled for February 4 in Chattogram, with a reserve day confirmed on February 5.
The final will also be played in Chattogram on February 6 with February 7 set aside as a reserve day.
Groups:
Group A: India, Ireland, West Indies and Nepal
Group B: South Africa, New Zealand, Pakistan and Samoa
Group C: Australia, Bangladesh, Nigeria and the United Arab Emirates (UAE)
Group D: England, Sri Lanka, the United States of America (USA) and Scotland.

briefs.headline: Captain Iyer says Vaibhav Sooryavanshi must be patient for national opportunities
briefs.deck: It's important that a talent like him is always happy around the dressing room. And he is very young. He has more years to get opportunities. It's not like he can walk in straight away. Because our openers are also scoring consistently. And they also won the World Cup," Iyer said during the press conference ahead of the first T20I in Hagley Oval
briefs.bodyText:
India captain Shreyas Iyer has emphasised that teenage batting sensation Vaibhav Sooryavanshi will have to be patient for opportunities in the national side, saying the 15-year-old has plenty of time to establish himself despite his impressive performances in the Indian Premier League (IPL).
"It's important that a talent like him is always happy around the dressing room. And he is very young. He has more years to get opportunities. It's not like he can walk in straight away. Because our openers are also scoring consistently. And they also won the World Cup," Iyer said during the press conference ahead of the first T20I in Hagley Oval.
Sooryavanshi, who made his international debut for India in July, has attracted considerable attention with his aggressive batting but has been used sparingly against top opposition despite his exploits in the IPL. The left-handed opener made his IPL debut in 2025 at the age of 14 years and 23 days before scoring his maiden century in the competition just nine days later.
In eight T20 internationals, Sooryavanshi has scored 246 runs at an average of 30.75 and a strike rate of 186.36, including two half-centuries. His IPL numbers have been even more impressive, with an average of 44 and a strike rate of nearly 229. India's established opening options, Sanju Samson and Abhishek Sharma, have also been contributing consistently.
Since July, Samson has averaged 25 at a strike rate of 172, while Abhishek has averaged 30 at a strike rate of 200. Iyer, however, believes the ongoing tour of New Zealand will provide Sooryavanshi with valuable experience, irrespective of how many matches he plays. "So, if you see, when he is coming overseas, he will get a fair idea of how to play on these particular wickets. So, next time whenever he comes in these conditions, he will be very well prepared. And he will also get motivation to come here and make runs. And he can also instruct other youngsters who will come for the first time," Iyer said.
India arrived in New Zealand on Tuesday (October 20) for a 40-day tour featuring five T20Is, five one-day internationals and two Test matches. The tour also marks 100 years of sporting ties between the two countries. The five-match T20I series begins at Hagley Oval in Christchurch on Thursday, with Sooryavanshi among the options available to India as they prepare to face New Zealand in conditions that could offer opportunities for aggressive strokeplay.
India have recalled experienced seamer Bhuvneshwar Kumar after a four-year absence from the T20I side, while pace spearhead Jasprit Bumrah has been rested as part of workload management following his involvement in India's Asian Games gold-medal-winning campaign in Japan.
New Zealand, meanwhile, will be without Will O'Rourke, Mark Chapman and Zak Foulkes for the T20I series. Josh Clarkson and Blair Tickner have been brought into the squad as replacements for Chapman and Foulkes.The hosts will look to Finn Allen and Tim Seifert to provide explosive starts at the top of the order as they prepare to take on the reigning T20 world champions.

briefs.headline: India’s tour of New Zealand: on a wing and a prayer
briefs.deck: In their backyard, where pace is the king and spin a sideshow at best, the Kiwis have the personnel and the craft to put India through the wringer in the red-ball variant
briefs.bodyText:
The last time India travelled to New Zealand for a full tour, Virat Kohli was still the all-format captain and ruling the batting seas in all three versions. Shubman Gill had yet to make his Test debut, masks were associated with privacy (primarily) than health reasons, and the COVID-19 pandemic was just about beginning to send shock waves across the world.
That was in early 2020 – India played five Twenty20 Internationals, three One-Day Internationals and two Tests between January 29 and March 2 – when, as then head coach Ravi Shastri cheekily (?) pointed out, the tour ended in a 5-5 scoreline. Cute as that pronouncement was, there is no denying the fact that having started the journey convincingly with a 5-0 romp in the T20Is (including back-to-back Super Over triumphs), India were brushed aside in the next five matches.
Chastening loss
The most chastening of the defeats came in the Test series; India went down by 10 wickets in the first Test in Wellington and by seven in Christchurch (coincidentally, this year too, the tour winds down with Tests at these two venues in the same sequence), topping 200 just once in four innings. It was a bitter reality check for a team flying high on its 2-1 conquest of Australia in Australia just 14 months previously, a crushing blow that was the start of Kohli’s spectacular fall from grace in the longer format.
More than six and a half years later, with vastly changed personnel, India will attempt to secure their first Test win on Kiwi soil since 2009, when Mahendra Singh Dhoni led the team to a much-awaited 1-0 series victory. Since that Test win at Hamilton’s Seddon Park in March that year, the Indians have been winless in six matches, losing the last four, and therefore have a mountain to climb in their bid to end a long drought and wend themselves back into World Test Championship contention.
New Zealand in New Zealand are a formidable proposition even for the most experienced of Test sides, and India aren’t exactly flash on that commodity following the retirements of Kohli, Rohit Sharma and R. Ashwin after and during the tour of Australia in 2024-25. There is promise aplenty and K.L. Rahul, the vice-captain, and Ravindra Jadeja stand as firm bridges between the glorious past and the potentially bright future, Gill has his work cut out.
India are meandering mid-table following a string of underwhelming performances in the five-day format and must win at least five of their remaining seven Tests to stand any chance of making a pitch for the WTC finals. Considering two of them are in New Zealand and five at home against Australia between January and March, it will be no exaggeration to state that India are facing a second league exit in as many cycles after having made the final on the two previous occasions, in which case one would expect the pressure on head coach Gautam Gambhir to mount, at least in theory.
After a roaring start to the Gill era in England when, with a side that had very little first-hand taste of Test cricket overseas, India came away with an honourable 2-2 draw, the road has been rocky and arduous. A 2-0 win against West Indies at home was cancelled out by a similar drubbing, also at home, at the hands of WTC winners South Africa last November. India did win in Sri Lanka in August, but a 1-0 scoreline from two matches hasn’t done their cause too many favours, which is why they now find themselves teetering on the brink of early elimination, hanging on to the edge of the precipice with fraying, chipped fingernails.
Sparking interest, debate
But the Test series is a long way away for the time being – just under four weeks to go for the first game at the Basin Reserve, to be more exact. Before that, there is the small matter of five T20Is (starting in Christchurch on Thursday), followed by five ODIs which will generate greater interest simply because of the two stalwarts whose progress and presence has sparked tremendous interest and debate.
Let’s focus first on the T20Is, and the latest chapter in a book that is becoming unmanageably thick with meaningless words and disjointed sentences. In the middle of a gruelling, demanding run that has seen them play in three different continents in the last five months, Shreyas Iyer’s boys face a gun side that came out second best in the T20 World Cup final between the teams in Ahmedabad in March. India have seen a shake-up of sorts that has resulted in them moving past title-winning captain Suryakumar Yadav.
Shreyas has been given the responsibility of steering the ship, possibly till the next World Cup to be jointly hosted by New Zealand and Australia in two years’ time. Apart from getting early insights into what to expect at the World Cup, to be held at the same time of the year, there is little to gain from these five matches that, coupled with the five ODIs and the two Tests, make it the longest tour in terms of international matches (12) undertaken by any side to New Zealand.
Having steadfastly proclaimed their desire to excise themselves from the distant past and target the future, India have thrown a curveball by bringing the seasoned Bhuvneshwar Kumar back into the fray after nearly four years. The 36-year-old has 90 T20I wickets in 88 appearances and his economy of 6.96 is little short of outstanding, though his return testifies to a lack of potency in the bowling group in the absence of Jasprit Bumrah, whose workload is being carefully monitored so that he is available and raring to go for the big occasions.
Lack of bite and consistency
India’s support pace cast has been found badly wanting, their lack of bite and consistency thoroughly exposed during the white-ball series against West Indies earlier this month. Admittedly, they found little joy from the flat-as-pancake decks and dewy outfields that worked to their detriment, but even so, the cause for concern was so overwhelming that they had to go back to the past to ensure the immediate future isn’t shot. Perhaps, some of it has to do with the fact that Ajit Agarkar is no longer the chief selector. Equally, much of it is a quick-fix arrangement; at this point, it isn’t clear if Bhuvneshwar figures in the long-term plans or not, but there is no disputing the fact that his presence will lend the cutting edge so conspicuously absent when Bumrah isn’t around.
Bhuvneshwar’s first bowl in international cricket since November 2022 was delayed after the final T20I against West Indies in Bengaluru was washed out last Saturday, and he will be itching to hit the ground running in the same country where he played his last T20I. He should relish the conditions in New Zealand – an 8.00 p.m. local time start with summer yet to fully set in won’t hurt either – and if he and Arshdeep Singh can strike up a useful combine, it should take a lot of pressure off the other bowlers.
The T20Is should serve as the appetiser to the feast that encompasses two main courses, starting with the first of five ODIs in Auckland on November 4. In some ways, this is the start of the homestretch of preparations for the 50-over World Cup in southern Africa in less than a year’s time. Conditions in New Zealand will largely mirror those that can be expected in South Africa and this will be a good run out for Gill’s boys, who will again seek to draw inspiration from the gargantuan presence of Rohit and Kohli, inarguably two of the greatest white-ball batters of all time.
The debate over their futures laid to rest for the time being (at least) after a stellar run of scores that have exploded unfounded doubts about their commitment to the cause, Rohit and Kohli will use this opportunity to continue to entertain, enthral and enjoy whatever time they have at the highest level. It’s not often that teams play five ODIs in a bilateral series anymore but given that the World Cup is the ultimate goal, it isn’t the worst thing that those involved in these discussions have pencilled in five matches. Of course, India have withdrawn several players, including skipper Gill, for the last two ODIs, given their proximity to the Test series to follow. But that will in no way devalue the last two-fifths of the faceoff because of the context as well as the fact that Rohit and Kohli will still be around to guide the team and to encourage and educate stand-in skipper Shreyas as and when the need arises.
Own business to tend to
While much of the focus will be on India, even more so than on the home side, New Zealand have their own business to tend to. They are currently ranked No. 2 in the WTC standings, only behind their great trans-Tasman rivals Australia, and won’t be unaware that a good result against the Indians will keep them firmly in the fray as they seek to emulate their heroics of the inaugural cycle when they defeated India in the final in Southampton. The Kiwis are also in the throes of transition, with former captain Kane Williamson no longer available for selection, but even though they tend to fly under the radar, they are always a formidable, competitive and skilful unit that will seek to maximise home advantage.
New Zealand aren’t the kind to rub into their opponents’ faces the fact that they crushed India 3-0 in India in October-November 2024, but then again, they don’t need to. The wounds from that unexpected hammering are still festering, the scars still all too visible. Conditions in Wellington and Christchurch will be vastly different from Pune and Mumbai where left-arm spinners Mitchell Santner and Ajaz Patel made merry. In their backyard, where pace is the king and spin a sideshow at best, the Kiwis have the personnel and the craft to put India through the wringer in the red-ball variant.
This Test tour will be a big examination of the techniques and temperaments of young left-handed top-order batters Yashasvi Jaiswal and Devdutt Padikkal. If they can come through this baptism by fire with their reputations intact, if not enhanced, India can derive comfort from the truism that there is reason to look forward to the future with optimism. By the time the Test series starts on November 19, though, there would have been no shortage of drama, that’s for sure.

briefs.headline: Gary Stead warns New Zealand against taking home advantage for granted
briefs.deck: Stead, currently head coach of Andhra’s Ranji Trophy team, believes India’s ability to adapt to New Zealand’s bouncy surfaces will be crucial to their chances.
briefs.bodyText:
BENGALURU: Home advantage is losing its sheen in international cricket, with teams increasingly equipped to beat opponents in the latter's own backyard. Former head coach Gary Stead believes hosts New Zealand may not enjoy the edge they once did when India begin their tour with the T20 series beginning on Thursday, with the visitors’ improved pace attack and the ability to adapt to challenging conditions making them a formidable opponent.
The 54-year-old, who oversaw a successful phase in New Zealand cricket, including their World Test Championship triumph, said the days of exploiting an opponent’s perceived weakness were fading.
“Earlier, you played India and thought, ‘Oh, we’ll do a green track because they don’t have good seamers.’ Now they have quality seamers as well,” Stead said.
Referring to New Zealand’s 3-0 triumph in the 2024 Test series in India, he added: “The same way, when we came in 2024, we had quality spinners too. The whole idea of home advantage has disappeared a little bit around the world. Everyone has shown the competence to beat everyone else at any given time. So you’ve got to be on your game and be sharp.”
Stead, currently head coach of Andhra’s Ranji Trophy team, believes India’s ability to adapt to New Zealand’s bouncy surfaces will be crucial to their chances.
“The Indians are going to have to adapt to bouncy wickets, some of the bounciest possibly in the world. 
The wickets will have bounce and carry. If the Indian players can nullify New Zealand’s bowlers, then I think it’ll be a cracking series,” he said.
The Test matches, in particular, could pose the toughest challenge. Stead pointed to Hagley Oval in Christchurch and Basin Reserve Wellington as venues traditionally known for their extra bounce.
“It's very important for New Zealand. India are obviously an amazing Test side, and then we go to Australia and play, so there are six huge Tests coming up for New Zealand. But if you want to be judged against the best, you’ve got to compete against the best as well,” he said.
With Australia and South Africa also producing compelling Test cricket recently, Stead believes the influence of T20 cricket is increasingly visible in the longest format.
“I think the T20 format has allowed players a little bit more freedom in the way they play. And I think that’s rubbing off on Test cricket now as well,” he said.
Stead also called on the International Cricket Council (ICC) to explore more multi-format series, arguing that longer tours could help sustain interest across formats.
“Personally, I think the ICC should consider playing more multi-format series. Rather than teams coming and going very quickly and people forgetting about the series, it could be a little like the women’s Ashes, where they have multi-format scenarios. I really think it’s something that could take off,” he said.
However, he acknowledged that fitting longer tours into an increasingly crowded international calendar would be difficult, with teams constantly preparing for the next World Cup in one of the two white-ball formats.
